Scarborough.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Yorkshire Coast
s1loc: Scarborough is England's original seaside resort and one of the Yorkshire Coast's biggest visitor draws, split between the sandy South Bay and quieter North Bay. The clifftop Scarborough Castle commands the headland between the two bays, the working harbour lands fresh catch at the foot of the old town, and the Grade II* listed Spa with its 557-seat theatre anchors the South Bay seafront.

The leisure and activity layer is busy across the season, from the oriental-themed Peasholm Park with its boating lake and naval battles to Alpamare water park and Sea Life Scarborough out at Scalby Mills. The Scarborough North Bay Railway has run its miniature line since 1931, linking Peasholm to the Sea Life Centre, while cliff lifts, amusement arcades and the beaches keep operators working through the summer.

Heritage and culture run deep, led by the Rotunda Museum of 1829, the oldest purpose-built museum still in use in the country, and the Stephen Joseph Theatre, home to Britain's first theatre-in-the-round and long associated with Alan Ayckbourn. The clifftop Scarborough Open Air Theatre above North Bay is Europe's largest open-air venue, drawing big-name summer acts and filling the town's events calendar.

The visitor trade rests on a deep base of seafront hotels, guest houses and Bed and Breakfast along the Esplanade and both bays, with tour operators and guides working the coast and the North York Moors beyond. Rail links to York and the wider network bring day-trippers in, and the surrounding coastline at Filey and Whitby gives operators a strong seasonal draw alongside Bridlington, Beverley and York.

Orpington.region: Orpington and the south of the Bromley borough
Orpington.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Bromley borough
s1loc: Orpington sits at the green southern edge of the London Borough of Bromley, where suburban day-trips meet the North Downs countryside. Crofton Roman Villa, discovered in 1926 and now under cover beside the station, is one of the area's marquee heritage draws, while the Grade II listed Priory Gardens with its Italianate and Arts and Crafts grounds frame the spot where the River Cray rises.

The leisure and activity layer reaches well beyond the town, from High Elms Country Park with its 250 acres of woodland, nature centre and BEECHE visitor centre to Goddington Park and the wider North Downs trails. The Walnuts leisure centre with its 33-metre pool serves the centre, and Crystal Palace Park to the north, with its famous Victorian dinosaur sculptures of 1854, pulls visitors in from across the borough.

Heritage and culture run from the Bull pub and the old village core to the seven-screen Odeon at the rebuilt Walnuts centre, with the Stone Age and Iron Age finds at Goddington Park and Poverest pointing to deep local history. The Priory itself houses the Bromley Museum collection, and the parks and gardens host seasonal events that fill the local calendar through the warmer months.

The visitor trade leans on hotels and guest houses across Orpington and neighbouring Bromley, with guides and operators working the North Downs, Down House at nearby Downe and the Kent countryside on the doorstep. Fast rail links into London and out towards the coast carry day-trippers both ways, and the green belt gives operators a steady seasonal draw alongside Bromley, Sidcup and Sevenoaks.

Wallasey.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Wirral peninsula
s1loc: Wallasey occupies the north-eastern tip of the Wirral, and its seaside resort of New Brighton is the marquee draw, with sandy beaches on the Irish Sea and the mouth of the Mersey and one of the UK's longest promenades. Fort Perch Rock, a coastal battery built between 1825 and 1829 to guard the estuary, now works as a heritage attraction, and the 1830 New Brighton Lighthouse stands as one of the peninsula's best-known landmarks.

The leisure and activity layer centres on the New Brighton seafront, where the Art Deco New Palace amusement arcade and fairground, the Riverside Bowl and the Marine Lake draw families across the season. The promenade is a long, level route for walking and cycling with views over to the Liverpool waterfront, and the beaches and dunes at Leasowe and Wallasey Embankment add open-air days out through the summer.

Heritage and culture run through the Floral Pavilion, Wirral's largest theatre, rebuilt in 2008 with a conference centre as the first phase of New Brighton's regeneration, with a full calendar of touring and local shows. The Black Pearl pirate ship built from driftwood on the beach, the Leasowe Lighthouse and Wallasey's old village core add to a local story that mixes resort history with the wider Wirral heritage.

The visitor trade rests on guest houses, Bed and Breakfast and hotels across New Brighton and Wallasey, with operators and guides working the Mersey ferries, the Wirral Way and the peninsula's coast. The Mersey ferry, Merseyrail and the tunnels carry day-trippers in from Liverpool, and the wider Wirral coastline gives the trade a steady seasonal draw alongside Birkenhead, Bebington and Bromborough.

Hayes.region: Hayes and the west of Hillingdon
Hayes.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of west Hillingdon
s1loc: Hayes in the London Borough of Hillingdon carries a striking industrial heritage, led by the Old Vinyl Factory off Blyth Road, the former EMI works where The Beatles' records, including Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band, were pressed and where albums carried the words Hayes, Middlesex. The Grade II listed Enterprise House of 1912 and the Wallis, Gilbert and Partners buildings anchor a marquee heritage quarter now reborn as a cultural and events destination.

The leisure and activity layer is built around green space and water, from Lake Farm Country Park with its sixty acres of green belt beside the Grand Union Canal to Stockley Country Park, a restored landscape listed Grade II in 2020. The Grand Union Canal threads through the town centre with its towpaths, the Botwell Green sports and leisure centre offers pools and courts, and the wider Colne Valley trails sit close by.

Heritage and culture centre on the Beck Theatre, a 600-seat venue of 1977 set in parkland beside the Norman Leddy Memorial Gardens, alongside the annual Old Vinyl Factory Festival that celebrates the town's recording past. St Mary the Virgin church in Hayes village, the canalside conservation area and Brunel University at nearby Uxbridge add to a cultural and events offer that fills the local calendar through the year.

The visitor trade is shaped above all by its position on the doorstep of Heathrow, with a deep base of airport hotels and Bed and Breakfast across Hayes and Harlington. Hayes and Harlington station, the Elizabeth line and the canal carry visitors and crews in and out, and the town's mix of business parks, attractions and West London links gives operators a steady year-round draw alongside Hounslow, Uxbridge and Feltham.

Aylesbury.region: Aylesbury and the Vale of Buckinghamshire
Aylesbury.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Vale of Aylesbury
s1loc: Aylesbury is the county town of Buckinghamshire and the gateway to the Vale, with the National Trust's Waddesdon Manor as its marquee draw - a neo-Renaissance Rothschild mansion of 1874 to 1889 set in formal parterre gardens by Elie Laine. In the town itself the Buckinghamshire County Museum, built around a 500-year-old timber-framed guildhall, anchors a historic core around the cobbled Market Square and St Mary's church.

The leisure and activity layer runs from the Roald Dahl Children's Gallery, set in a former coach house with its Giant Peach and BFG exhibits, to the green spaces of Vale Park and the canal basin at the head of the Aylesbury Arm of the Grand Union Canal. The surrounding Chiltern Hills, the Ridgeway National Trail and Coombe Hill give walkers and outdoor operators open country a short drive from the centre.

Heritage and culture centre on the modern Waterside Theatre, which stages West End musicals, comedy and concerts, alongside the King's Head, a National Trust medieval coaching inn, and the Roald Dahl trail that links the town to Great Missenden. The Market Square statue of David Bowie, the Friars music heritage and a busy programme of markets and festivals keep the events calendar full through the year.

The visitor trade rests on hotels, inns and Bed and Breakfast across the town and the Vale, with guides and tour operators working Waddesdon, the Chilterns and the National Trust estates nearby. Aylesbury's rail links to Marylebone and the road network carry day-trippers in, and the surrounding countryside, gardens and stately homes give the trade a strong seasonal draw alongside High Wycombe, Bicester and Hemel Hempstead.

Hereford.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Herefordshire
s1loc: Hereford is the cathedral city of Herefordshire, and the golden-stone Hereford Cathedral is its marquee draw, home to the medieval Mappa Mundi, the largest surviving map of its kind, and the world's biggest surviving chained library. The half-timbered streets, the Jacobean Old House on High Town and the banks of the River Wye frame a historic core that pulls visitors into the heart of the Welsh Marches.

The leisure and activity layer follows the River Wye, the fifth longest river in Britain and a protected Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, with canoeing, rowing and riverside walks at Castle Green and the Victoria Bridge. The Bishop's Meadow and the riverside paths, together with the surrounding Wye Valley and the Black Mountains beyond, give activity and outdoor operators a steady draw across the warmer months.

Heritage and culture run from the Cider Museum, set in the former Bulmers factory with its original champagne cider cellars, to the Black and White House Museum tracing Jacobean life, and on to the Courtyard on Edgar Street, the city's main arts venue with a 436-seat auditorium. The Hereford River Carnival, the Three Choirs Festival in rotation and a busy markets calendar keep the events programme full through the year.

The visitor trade rests on hotels, coaching inns and Bed and Breakfast across the city and the county, with guides and tour operators working the cider trails, the Wye Valley and the border country. Rail links towards Worcester and Newport carry day-trippers in, and the surrounding countryside, orchards and market towns give the trade a strong seasonal draw alongside Malvern, Worcester and Kidderminster.

Merthyr Tydfil.region: Merthyr Tydfil and the South Wales Valleys
Merthyr Tydfil.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the South Wales Valleys
s1loc: Merthyr Tydfil sits at the head of the Taff valley on the edge of the Bannau Brycheiniog National Park, and its marquee draw is Cyfarthfa Castle, the castellated mansion of 1825 built for ironmaster William Crawshay II and now home to the Cyfarthfa Castle Museum and Art Gallery. The town's ironmaking story, the surviving Ynysfach engine house and the dramatic Pontsarn and Cefn Coed viaducts mark it as the cradle of the industrial Valleys.

The leisure and activity layer is led by BikePark Wales, the UK's leading mountain biking destination with more than forty trails across an 850-hectare site, and the Brecon Mountain Railway, which climbs into the national park along the old Brecon and Merthyr line. The traffic-free Taff Trail crosses the viaducts north of the town, and Cyfarthfa Park, the reservoirs and the mountain country give outdoor operators a year-round draw.

Heritage and culture centre on Redhouse, the arts complex in the Grade II* listed Old Town Hall, alongside the cottages of Chapel Row where composer Joseph Parry was born and the wider story told at Cyfarthfa. The town's choral and chapel traditions, the Merthyr Rising festival and a busy programme of events at Redhouse and in the parks keep the cultural calendar full across the seasons.

The visitor trade rests on hotels, inns and Bed and Breakfast across the town and the surrounding Valleys, with guides and operators working the national park gateway, the bike park and the Taff Trail. Road links down to Cardiff and the rail line into the Valleys network carry day-trippers in, and the mountains, reservoirs and Pen y Fan within reach give the trade a strong seasonal draw alongside Aberdare, Pontypridd and Caerphilly.
